title: Semiparametric modeling of age at achieving developmental milestones after prenatal exposure to methylmercury in the Seychelles child development study.
ehr_evidence: The Seychelles Child Development Study (SCDS) is an ongoing longitudinal study of the effects of prenatal mercury exposure through maternal fish consumption on neurodevelopmental outcomes in children; exposure was measured as the mean total mercury concentration in segments of maternal hair, and developmental milestone ages were recorded via face-to-face interview with the child's parent/caregiver at 19 months.
summary: A semiparametric (generalized additive model) analysis of 779 Seychellois children in the SCDS cohort evaluating the effect of prenatal methylmercury exposure (maternal hair mercury) on age at walking and age at first words.
key_findings: Very slight delays (<1 day) in walking were seen at mercury levels from 0 to 7 ppm but did not persist at higher exposure levels, making it difficult to conclude a cause-and-effect relationship.
There was no evidence for any association between prenatal mercury exposure and age at talking.
In the reduced model with a mercury-by-sex interaction, the overall smooth term for mercury was significant for males (p=0.028) but not for females (p=0.74).
In the reduced model without interaction, the smoothed mercury term was a significant predictor of age at walking (p=0.036), with the nonlinear component significant (p=0.045).
The estimated change in age at walking from a 1 to 5 ppm increase in exposure was +0.04 months and from 5 to 15 ppm was -0.03 months.
The effect sizes were small, on the order of ±1 day, and the apparent increase in age at walking at low mercury levels may be spurious.
pathologies_diseases: developmental milestone delays (age at walking and talking)
population: 779 Seychellois children from the main SCDS cohort, evaluated at 19 months of age (738 available for testing), in Seychelles
limitations: Developmental milestone data relied on maternal recall via face-to-face interview, introducing potential recall bias.
Effect sizes were very small (on the order of ±1 day) and the low-level effect may be spurious.
Sparse data at higher exposure levels (>15 ppm) limited estimation of the dose-response relationship.
